supported_claims.text: 手 is an indivisible pictograph of a hand. Bronze forms are described as showing branching fingers above and an arm or palm below; the exact anatomy is an interpretation. No separate internal components or sound element are supported.

The earliest graph evidence identified in the dossier is from Western Zhou bronze materials. Those occurrences have no verified semantic context or individual earliest inscription date, so they establish early graphic use rather than a securely dated first use meaning “hand.”

The hand meaning is supported by the pictographic analysis and later lexicographic evidence. Shuowen glosses the character as 拳 (“fist”), while its commentator treats hand and fist as mutually explanatory; this does not establish that “fist” was the original meaning or set a semantic chronology.

Transmitted classical citations attest 手 in the hand sense; later dictionary citations also record uses for a skilled person, handwriting, and the verb “hold.” The dossier does not establish dates or a pathway connecting these later uses.
Baxter–Sagart gives 手 as Old Chinese *n̥uʔ and Middle Chinese syuwX. The dossier proposes no phonetic component for this pictographic graph.

disagreements.text: One paleographic account describes the lower part of the bronze graph as an arm, while another describes fingers, palm, and arm. The sources agree on a hand pictograph but do not settle its precise graphic anatomy.

The cited paleographic discussions report no oracle-bone graph 手 and distinguish other hand-shaped graphs; the dossier therefore does not support treating 手 as securely attested in oracle-bone inscriptions.

limitations.text: The dossier identifies Western Zhou bronze examples but verifies neither an individual earliest inscription date nor semantic contexts for those occurrences. Its evidence for the hand meaning comes from graphic interpretation and lexicographic analysis.

The classical examples and later senses are transmitted dictionary citations, not independently dated excavated attestations. Their chronological order and semantic transitions remain unestablished here.

The dossier does not establish the spoken-word history of 手 or the proposed comparisons with Proto-Sino-Tibetan vocabulary, Burmese, or 收; these proposals do not alter the supported pictographic analysis.
